name: MyoBloc / NeuroBloc (rimabotulinumtoxinB)

lead: MyoBloc (US) or NeuroBloc (EU) is rimabotulinumtoxinB, a type B botulinum toxin approved for cervical dystonia. Like type A products, it relaxes the muscles under dynamic wrinkles, which is why clinicians have explored it for forehead, frown and crow's-feet lines.
Small trials found improvement in facial lines with onset within days and an effect lasting about eight weeks, shorter than usual for type A [5][7].

paras: It is injected by clinicians into facial muscles, as with other toxins; most aesthetic practice uses type A brands instead. Type B has been used mainly when patients are resistant to type A.

Reviews report more regional and systemic anticholinergic effects than type A, such as dry mouth, accommodation difficulty and dysphagia, and injection pain [1]. Toxin can spread beyond the injection site, and the FDA added boxed warnings for this in 2009 [13].

chain: Dynamic lines on forehead, frown and eye area soften
angle.text: Injected into expression muscles, type B toxin produced improvement in lines within about 72 hours in a small study, lasting about eight weeks [5]. It is used mostly when type A is not an option.

lead: Rimabotulinumtoxin B is marketed as Myobloc in the US and Neurobloc in the EU. The FDA approved it for cervical dystonia in December 2000, and it has been used since 1999 for dystonia, hyperhidrosis, spasticity, sialorrhoea and other conditions, as well as cosmetic applications [1][2].

Botulinum toxins block the nerve signal to a muscle, softening wrinkles caused by repeated expression. Aesthetic practice centres on type A products such as Botox, Dysport and Xeomin [3]. Type B targets a different SNARE protein and is not interchangeable with type A, with its own dosing [2].

Cosmetic research on type B is small: a 24-patient study and a randomised pilot trial in crow's feet [4][5]. A reviewer concluded its effects are comparable to type A, with a different side-effect profile [1].

paras: Clinicians have injected type B into the corrugator, orbicularis oculi and frontalis for hyperkinetic facial lines [4], and a pilot trial tested it in crow's feet [5]. Aesthetic overviews, however, describe the three type A products as the available aesthetic toxins [3].
Its established indication is cervical dystonia, including patients who have become resistant to type A [6][7]. It has also been studied in hemifacial spasm [8] and craniofacial hyperhidrosis [9].

Type B produces more regional and systemic anticholinergic effects than type A, including dry mouth, accommodation difficulty, conjunctival irritation, reduced sweating and dysphagia [1]. Toxin spread from the injection site can weaken unintended muscles, and the FDA added boxed warnings in 2009 [2]. Antibody-related therapy failure has been examined in de novo cervical dystonia [10].
Pharmacology reviews compare the therapeutic toxin preparations and their serotypes [11][12]. Type A and type B act on different SNARE proteins, and products are not interchangeable [2].

A 2002 trial treated 24 patients in the corrugator, orbicularis oculi or frontalis; wrinkle scores were statistically better, with onset within 72 hours and an effect lasting 8 weeks [4]. A 2003 double-blind randomised pilot study tested Myobloc in crow's feet versus placebo [5]. Other trials cover cervical dystonia [6][10], hemifacial spasm [8] and hyperhidrosis [9].

lore.intro: Type B toxin is rarely discussed in looksmaxxing communities; the only mention found is a 2002 T Nation thread titled "Myostatin inhibitor" in which "Myoblock" appears in a joke about looks [13].

claims.claim: Botulinum toxin products can be used as wrinkle relaxers.
